## Abstract

Write a brief one-paragraph abstract that describes the contents of your write-up.

## Dataset

The data came from Hewitson et al. (2021), who used serum proteomics to identify blood biomarkers for Austim Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in young boys. Blood samples were collected from 154 boys aged 18 months to 8 years: 76 with ASD and 78 typically developing (TD) boys. The level of 1317 proteins were measured for each subject. The dataset also records each subject's group (ASD or TD) and for boys with ASD, and ADOS severity score. In the published analysis, 192 of the proteins failed quality control, which left 1125 proteins. However, our analysis includes 1317.

Preprocessing was conducted in three steps, each applied to every protein. First, a $log_{10}$ transformation reduced the strong right skew in the raw protein levels. Second, the log transformed values were standardized to $z$-scores so that proteins measured on different scales could be compared. Third, outliers were trimmed by capping the standardized values to the range \[-3,3\], which limits the influence of more extreme measurements on the analysis.

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

```{r load-raw-data}
#getting protein names
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
var_names <- read_csv(here("data", "biomarker-raw.csv"), 
                     col_names = F, 
                     n_max = 2, 
                     col_select = -(1:2)) |>
  t() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(name = V1, 
         abbreviation = V2) |>
  na.omit()

#load in data
biomarker_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "biomarker-raw.csv"),
                          skip = 2,
                          col_select = -2L,
                          col_names = c("group",
                                        "empty",
                                        pull(var_names, abbreviation),
                                        "ados"),
                          na = c("-", "")) |>
  filter(!is.na(group)) |>
  select(group, ados, everything())


```

```{r, fig.width= 8, fig.height= 10}
#picking 4 random proteins
set.seed(2026)

protein_cols <- setdiff(names(biomarker_raw), c("group","ados"))
chosen <- sample(protein_cols, 4)

hist_data <- biomarker_raw |>
  select(all_of(chosen)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "protein", values_to = "raw") |>
  mutate(log10 = log10(raw)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(raw, log10), names_to = "scale", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("raw", "log10")))

hist_plot <- ggplot(hist_data, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(vars(protein, scale), scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "protein level", y = "count",
       title = "raw vs. log10 protein levels")

hist_plot

ggsave(here("results", "figures", "q1-raw-vs-log-histograms.png"),
       plot = hist_plot, width = 8, height = 10, dpi = 300)

```

```{r skewness}
skew <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}

skew_summary <- tibble(
  protein = protein_cols,
  raw = map_dbl(biomarker_raw[protein_cols], skew),
  log10 = map_dbl(biomarker_raw[protein_cols], ~skew(log10(.x))),
  mean_gt_median = map_lgl(biomarker_raw[protein_cols],
                           ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) > median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))

skew_table <- skew_summary |>
  summarise(median_skew_raw = median(raw),
            median_skew_log10 = median(log10),
            pct_right_skewed_raw = mean(raw > 0) * 100,
            pct_mean_above_median = mean(mean_gt_median) * 100)

skew_table

write_csv(skew_table, here("results", "tables", "q1-skewness-summary.csv"))

```

We compared the raw and $log_{10}$ transformed distributions of four randomly selected proteins. The raw levels are strongly right skewed, with most values near the low end and a long tail of large values. After the $log_{10}$ transformation, the distributions are roughly symmetric. This holds across all proteins: the median skewness drops from around 2.25 to around 0.83, and 96.735% of proteins are right skewed on the raw scale. Since the later steps such as t-tests, z-scores, and trimming at $\pm3$) work best on symmetric data, the log transformation keeps a few extreme values from dominating the analysis.

Task 4

```{r}
#| include: false
#in class analysis
save(list = 'biomarker_clean', 
     file = here('data', 'biomarker-clean.RData'))

#biomarker_clean
## MULTIPLE TESTING
####################

# function to compute tests
test_fn <- function(.df){
  t_test(.df, 
         formula = level ~ group,
         order = c('ASD', 'TD'),
         alternative = 'two-sided',
         var.equal = F)
}

ttests_out <- biomarker_clean %>%
  # drop ADOS score
  select(-ados) %>%
  # arrange in long format
  pivot_longer(-group, 
               names_to = 'protein', 
               values_to = 'level') %>%
  # nest by protein
  nest(data = c(level, group)) %>% 
  # compute t tests
  mutate(ttest = map(data, test_fn)) %>%
  unnest(ttest) %>%
  # sort by p-value
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  # multiple testing correction
  mutate(m = n(),
         hm = log(m) + 1/(2*m) - digamma(1),
         rank = row_number(),
         p.adj = m*hm*p_value/rank)

# select significant proteins
proteins_s1 <- ttests_out %>%
  slice_min(p.adj, n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)

## RANDOM FOREST
##################

# store predictors and response separately
predictors <- biomarker_clean %>%
  select(-c(group, ados))

response <- biomarker_clean %>% pull(group) %>% factor()

# fit RF
set.seed(101422)
rf_out <- randomForest(x = predictors, 
                       y = response, 
                       ntree = 1000, 
                       importance = T)

# check errors
rf_out$confusion

# compute importance scores
proteins_s2 <- rf_out$importance %>% 
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(protein = rownames(rf_out$importance)) %>%
  slice_max(MeanDecreaseGini, n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)

## LOGISTIC REGRESSION
#######################

# select subset of interest
proteins_sstar <- intersect(proteins_s1, proteins_s2)

biomarker_sstar <- biomarker_clean %>%
  select(group, any_of(proteins_sstar)) %>%
  mutate(class = (group == 'ASD')) %>%
  select(-group)

# partition into training and test set
set.seed(101422)
biomarker_split <- biomarker_sstar %>%
  initial_split(prop = 0.8)

# fit logistic regression model to training set
fit <- glm(class ~ ., 
           data = training(biomarker_split), 
           family = 'binomial')

# evaluate errors on test set
class_metrics <- metric_set(sensitivity, 
                            specificity, 
                            accuracy,
                            roc_auc)


# Evaluate errors on test set cleanly
class_metrics <- metric_set(sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, roc_auc)

test_eval <- testing(biomarker_split) %>%
  add_predictions(fit, type = 'response') %>%
  mutate(
    truth    = factor(class, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE")),
    estimate = factor(pred > 0.5, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))
  )

test_eval %>%
  class_metrics(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, pred, event_level = 'second')
```

```{r}
# Task 4: Simpler Panel

# Existing baseline panel
print(proteins_sstar)

# Extract top 3 proteins from proteins_sstar using existing importance scores
rf_imp_df <- rf_out$importance %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(protein = rownames(rf_out$importance))

proteins_simple <- rf_imp_df %>%
  filter(protein %in% proteins_sstar) %>%
  slice_max(MeanDecreaseGini, n = 3) %>%
  pull(protein)

# Simpler panel proteins after selecting top 3 based on importance scores
print(proteins_simple)

# Fit logistic regression on the same training data using the simple panel
simple_formula <- as.formula(paste("class ~", paste(paste0("`", proteins_simple, "`"), collapse = " + ")))

fit_simple <- glm(
  simple_formula,
  data = training(biomarker_split),
  family = 'binomial'
)

# Evaluate the simpler model on the same test data
test_eval_simple <- testing(biomarker_split) %>%
  add_predictions(fit_simple, type = 'response') %>%
  mutate(
    truth    = factor(class, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE")),
    estimate = factor(pred > 0.5, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))
  )

# Benchmark Comparison Table
metrics_baseline <- test_eval %>%
  class_metrics(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, pred, event_level = 'second') %>%
  mutate(model = "Baseline (5 Proteins)", panel_size = length(proteins_sstar))

metrics_simple <- test_eval_simple %>%
  class_metrics(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, pred, event_level = 'second') %>%
  mutate(model = "Simpler Panel (3 Proteins)", panel_size = length(proteins_simple))

benchmark_table <- bind_rows(metrics_baseline, metrics_simple) %>%
  select(model, panel_size, .metric, .estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) %>%
  select(model, panel_size, roc_auc, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity)

print(benchmark_table)
```

To find a simpler predictive panel, we isolated the top three proteins (DERM, IgD, and RELT) from the baseline five-protein consensus set based on their Random Forest Gini impurity scores and evaluated them via logistic regression on the same train/test split. Despite a reduction in panel size, the three-protein model achieved higher classification performance and ROCAUC compared to the in-class baseline, demonstrating that the secondary markers (eIF-4H and TSP4) contributed mostly redundant variance. The baseline proteins had a ROCAUC of 0.883 and an accuracy of 0.774 while the simple panel of proteins had a ROCAU of 0.892 and an accuracy of 0.806.
